question: How does Deb Liu explain treating product growth as a “game of inches,” and why does she favor shipping many small experiments over waiting for a perfect plan?
expected_points: Small improvements can compound into substantial growth over time.
Shipping many experiments helps teams learn what works and what doesn’t.
Improving the experiments’ success rate creates more wins without requiring a perfect plan.

answer.summary: Liu says growth usually comes from compounding small improvements, not one dramatic leap. Shipping many hypotheses in cycles creates both wins and learning, so teams can improve their success rate instead of waiting for a perfect plan.

sections.heading: Growth as a game of inches
sections.content: Rather than searching only for a huge step-change, Liu recommends looking for small, repeatable gains: moving something 1% faster each week, or making single-digit improvements that add up over time. Product-led growth means finding aha moments and small opportunities that can change user choices. Her example is Facebook adding a “create an ad” link beside ads: a simple signpost helped people find the ad flow and became a major growth driver. (Liu’s cited example.)

sections.heading: Why ship many small experiments
sections.content: Liu describes keeping a list of 100 payments-growth hypotheses, choosing the first 10 to work on, then the next 10 in sprint cycles; she says the ads and marketplace teams likewise looked for small changes that could add up. She argues it is acceptable if 80% of ideas fail: a team shipping 20 things with a 20% success rate gets four wins, as does a team shipping four things, but the larger set also reveals what does not work. At a 30% success rate, 20 attempts produce six wins—50% more than four—plus lessons to iterate on. She frames growth as a learning engine: use results to revise hypotheses and keep improving rather than overthinking a perfect battle plan. These numbers illustrate her comparison, not a guarantee of outcomes. (Synthesis of Liu’s recommendations.)

The reference and S2 compare 20 attempts at 20% success (four wins) with 20 at 30% (six wins), while contrasting this approach with overthinking a perfect plan. The answer covers both the benefit of improving the success rate and why not to wait for a perfect plan.

answer.summary: Deb Liu says growth usually comes from small gains that compound, not one magic leap. She favors shipping more hypotheses because failed attempts still teach the team, while successful ones add up to more output.

sections.heading: Growth as a game of inches
sections.content: Liu says companies often look for a huge step change, but growth can come from moving things 1% faster each week—or 3X through repeated 1% or 5% gains. Small changes can matter: she cites Facebook adding a “create an ad” link beside ads, which helped people find the ads flow and became a major growth driver. Across growth teams, she says, small improvements add up.

sections.heading: Why ship many experiments instead of waiting for a perfect plan
sections.content: Liu says teams can overthink the search for a perfect battle plan. In payments growth, her team worked from a list of 100 hypotheses, taking the first 10, then the next 10, in sprint cycles; she says they used the same approach for ads and marketplace. She considers it acceptable if 80% of ideas do not work. Her comparison: a team shipping 20 things with a 20% success rate gets four successes—the same as shipping four things if all four work—but also learns what failed. Raising the success rate from 20% to 30% yields six successes, or 50% more than four, alongside those lessons. She describes growth as a learning engine: use results to reiterate, change course, and improve.
